Gregory VII. Originally named Hildebrand, he reigned as pope from 1073 to 1085. A zealous reformer, he fought to establish the moral integrity and political independence of the papacy. He is best known for initiating the Gregorian Reforms and his epic struggle with Holy Roman Emperor Henry IV during the Investiture Controversy.

In 1075, he issued the Dictatus Papae, a compilation of 27 statements asserting absolute papal supremacy over both the Church and secular rulers, including the power to depose emperors. He excommunicated Holy Roman Emperor Henry IV over the right of secular rulers to appoint local church officials, initiating the decades-long Investiture Controversy. In 1077, he forced Henry IV to perform penance by waiting barefoot in the snow for three days outside the gates of the Castle of Canossa to have his excommunication lifted.

Gregory campaigned aggressively against simony, the buying and selling of church offices, and strictly enforced clerical celibacy. However, Henry IV invaded Rome, and Gregory died in exile in Salerno in 1085. His final words were famously remembered: "I have loved justice and hated iniquity; therefore, I die in exile." His assertions of absolute papal authority permanently altered medieval European geopolitics.
